title: Vaultlet dry-run runner: permissioned transactional admin utilities with step-sim simulation
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build a lightweight 'vaultlet' runner that wraps admin shortflows in a permissioned transactional runtime with first-class dry-run / step-sim support. Goal: provide on-call and support engineers with one-click simulated execution that mirrors production effects (checks, non-destructive validations, audit events) and a separate guarded path for real execution that acquires ephemeral creds from KMS-backed vaults. The runner should: 1) accept typed step manifests (task inputs, expected side-effects), 2) execute in simulation mode emitting simulated audit events and telemetry without changing resources, 3) support transactional commit/rollback semantics where applicable, 4) integrate with Console rollouts and RBAC (enforce policy gating), and 5) persist an execution proof artifact for audits and postmortems.
acceptance_criteria:
- CLI and Console button to run flow in dry-run mode with identical logs to live run
- Dry-run produces an 'execution proof' JSON that includes simulated audit events, decision branches, and expected token usage
- Live-run path fetches ephemeral credentials from configured KMS/vault and logs a commit marker to the audit store
- Step-level toggles allow skipping destructive steps in dry-run vs live-run parity tests
- CI integration: unit tests and e2e harness cover 80% of runner logic
technical_notes: Design decisions considered: (A) Full containerized sandbox vs step-sim engine; chose step-sim engine for low ops overhead and faster iteration. (B) Ephemeral creds: use KMS-signed short-lived tokens + Vault for secrets provisioning (trade-off: complexity for stronger auditability). (C) Transaction model: optimistic commit with compensating rollback functions provided by step authors. We'll add a later enhancement for two-phase commit on database-backed operations if needed.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Dry-run divergence from live-run due to external side-effects (3rd-party APIs). Mitigation: capture API response schemas and add fuzzed replay fixtures; require step authors to declare external calls. Risk: accidental privilege escalation via ephemeral tokens. Mitigation: enforce RBAC policy checks in the runner and require signed runflows for high-risk actions.
